I will estimate a causal effect using two-stage least squares: first-stage regresses metropolitan 2002–2006 house-price growth (treatment) on pre-determined housing supply elasticity (supply_elast) and baseline homeowner covariates, second-stage regresses the change in home-secured debt (as a share of 2002 home value, outcome) on the predicted price growth; standard errors clustered at the CBSA. Key variables are house price growth (2002–2006), the outcome change in home-secured debt/share of 2002 value, the instrument supply_elast, and baseline controls (age_2002, credit_score_2002, log home_value_2002, debt_2002, tenure_years and metro pre-2002 trends such as job growth and college-educated share) plus CBSA fixed effects. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because supply_elast correlates with long-run local demand and economic trends (the tight-land metros had faster job and college-educated growth) that could directly affect borrowing; I will mitigate this by controlling for pre-2002 metro trends, showing balance on observables, running placebo/specification tests (e.g., predicting non-housing secured borrowing and pre-period debt changes), and reporting weak-instrument-robust inference. As a robustness check in the state-coastal subset I will report IV estimates using permit_draw (the randomized permit suspension) with Anderson–Rubin confidence sets to reflect its weak first-stage.  

CANDIDATES:
supply_elast | plausible
permit_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: supply_elast

I will estimate the causal effect of trade (exports+imports as share of GDP) on log income per person using two-stage least squares, instrumenting trade with the gravity-predicted trade share (geo_trade) to exploit exogenous geographic variation in trade potential. Key variables are outcome = log income per person; treatment = trade_share (exports+imports / GDP); instrument = geo_trade; controls = log population, log land_area, landlocked, colony, region, and main language group (and other geography controls from the codebook as robustness covariates). Estimation: first stage regresses trade_share on geo_trade and controls (report first-stage F and partial R2), second stage regresses log income on predicted trade_share and controls, using heteroskedasticity-robust SEs and weak-instrument-robust inference (LIML or Anderson–Rubin) as needed. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because geo_trade may affect income directly through market access, resource endowments, or remoteness; I will mitigate this by conditioning on direct geographic covariates, conducting sensitivity/overidentification tests, comparing to OLS, and reporting robustness to alternative specifications. I will also consider the customs_draw pilot as an alternative instrument for a limited-sample robustness check but note it covers only 20 countries and has a weak first stage (F≈2).  
CANDIDATES:
geo_trade | plausible
customs_draw | doubtful
landlocked | violated
INSTRUMENT: geo_trade

I will estimate the causal effect of trade (exports+imports as share of GDP) on log income per person using two-stage least squares (2SLS) in the sub-sample exposed to the 1980 regional customs pilot, instrumenting country trade shares with the pilot random draw (customs_draw) and including controls (log population, log land_area, landlocked, colony, region, language, and geo_trade as a robustness control) to improve precision and address remaining imbalance. Key variables are: outcome = log income per person; treatment = trade share; instrument = customs_draw; controls listed above. I will report the first-stage F, use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin/CLE), and test balance and placebo outcomes to check the exclusion (the program memo states the draw changed nothing else). The main threat is that customs_draw is only observed for the 20 pilot countries and has a weak first-stage (F≈2), so estimates are imprecise, local to the pilot sample, and may lack external validity despite the random draw.  
CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | violated
landlocked | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares using the pilot random draw (customs_draw) that halved border fees for drawn countries as an instrument for trade openness (exports+imports as share of GDP), controlling for log population, log land_area, landlocked, colony, geo_trade, and region fixed effects to reduce confounding. Key variables are treatment = trade_share, outcome = log income per person (PPP), instrument = customs_draw, with robustness checks that include first-stage diagnostics, weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin / LIML), and reduced-form estimates. Because customs_draw is randomized within the 20-country pilot and “changed nothing else” by design, exclusion is plausible for those countries and gives a local causal effect of trade on income. The main threat is that the instrument is weak (first-stage F ≈ 2), yielding imprecise and potentially biased IV estimates and poor external validity beyond the pilot set; I will therefore report weak-IV-robust CIs and present bounds/alternative estimands if the instrument proves too weak. I will also test balance on observables in the pilot and check that results are not driven by post‑treatment policy changes in drawn countries.

CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | violated
landlocked | violated
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I'll estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares using the 1980 regional customs-pilot random draw (customs_draw) as an instrument for trade share (exports+imports as share of GDP) and the outcome log income per person, restricting the main IV sample to the countries in the pilot so the instrument is arguably randomized. Key variables: treatment = trade share, outcome = log GDP per person (PPP), instrument = customs_draw; I'll include covariates (population, land_area, landlocked, colony, region) to improve precision and to check balance. Because the agency memo reports the draw "changed nothing else" the exclusion is plausible, but the first-stage is weak (F≈2) and the pilot sample is small so I will report reduced-form, 2SLS, and weak‑IV‑robust confidence sets (Anderson–Rubin / conditional likelihood ratio) and present bounds where appropriate. The main threat is weak instrument bias and limited external validity since customs_draw is missing for almost all countries and identifies a local average treatment effect for pilot countries only. As a sensitivity check I will present results using geo_trade as an alternative instrument but treat those estimates as suspect because geography plausibly affects income through disease and other channels.

CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | violated
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will estimate the local causal effect of trade on log income per person using two-stage least squares, instrumenting the country trade share (exports+imports as share of GDP) with random assignment to the 1980 regional customs pilot (customs_draw) and restricting the sample to countries eligible for or comparable to the pilot to preserve the randomization. Key variables are the endogenous treatment trade_share (exports+imports/GDP), outcome log_income_per_person, instrument customs_draw, and pre-treatment controls for precision and balance checks (log population, log land_area, landlocked, region, colony). I will report first-stage strength and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or LIML) and show covariate balance and placebo outcomes to support exclusion. The main threat is a very weak first stage (F ≈ 2) and limited external validity from the small pilot sample, plus any post-randomization policy changes correlated with the draw. As robustness I will present estimates using geo_trade as an alternative instrument with careful controls for geography and disease proxies while noting its likely correlation with omitted geographic determinants of income. CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | doubtful
landlocked | violated
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of trade (exports+imports as share of GDP) on log income per person using two-stage least squares (2SLS) with the randomized customs_draw from the 1980 regional customs pilot as an instrument for trade: the draw exogenously cut border fees and raised trade shares for drawn countries. Key variables are treatment = trade share, outcome = log GDP per person (PPP), instrument = customs_draw, with controls for log population, log land area, landlocked, region, colony and language included for precision and to soak up remaining variation. I will report first-stage diagnostics (F-statistic), the reduced-form, OLS, and IV estimates, and use weak-IV-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin, LIML) because the first-stage is weak (F≈2). The main threat is weak instrument and limited external validity since customs_draw is observed for only 20 pilot countries; I will argue exclusion holds because the agency notes the draw "changed nothing else" but will test for other channels. Sensitivity checks will include bounding IV estimates, alternative controls, and presenting results both with and without the pilot-only sample.  
CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | violated
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will identify the causal effect with an instrumental-variables design that uses the 1980 regional customs pilot random draw (customs_draw) — which exogenously lowered border processing fees for drawn countries — to instrument country trade share (exports+imports as share of GDP) in a 2SLS framework. Key variables are treatment = trade share, outcome = log income per person, instrument = customs_draw, and I will condition only on pre-treatment covariates (log population, log land_area, landlocked, region, colony, language) to improve precision without inducing post-treatment bias. Because customs_draw is available only for the pilot subset and is weak (first-stage F ≈ 2), I will restrict analysis to the sample with instrument data, report first-stage diagnostics, and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin / conditional likelihood ratio and LIML) while interpreting estimates as a local average treatment effect for compliers. As a secondary check I will present results using geo_trade (gravity-predicted trade share) as an alternative instrument but treat it cautiously and report sensitivity/bounds because geography plausibly affects income through channels other than trade. The main threat is a weak and narrowly applicable instrument and potential violation of the exclusion restriction (e.g., the draw could have affected other outcomes or be correlated with regional shocks), so I will run balance/placebo tests, explore alternative instruments and specifications, and report weak-IV-robust confidence sets.  
CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | doubtful
landlocked | violated
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of trade on log income per person by two-stage least squares: first-stage regressing the treatment (exports+imports as share of GDP) on geo_trade (gravity-predicted trade) plus controls, and second-stage regressing log income on the fitted trade share; standard errors clustered at region and report first-stage F and IV diagnostics. Key variables: treatment = trade share (exports+imports/GDP), outcome = log GDP per person (PPP), instrument = geo_trade, controls = log population, log land_area, landlocked indicator, region fixed effects, colony and language dummies to soak up direct geographic and historical channels. I will assess instrument strength (first-stage F) and robustness by (a) using customs_draw as an alternative instrument in the pilot subsample and (b) adding controls for observable geography/resources and performing placebo outcome checks. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: geo_trade may affect income through non–trade channels (market access, resource endowments, coastal access) even after controls, so I will report bounds/sensitivity and emphasize that the IV estimate identifies a local effect for variation induced by geography. If geo_trade appears invalid in overidentification/sensitivity checks, I will fall back to reporting reduced-form associations and the randomized pilot (customs_draw) as a secondary, but limited-power, experiment.

CANDIDATES:
geo_trade | doubtful
customs_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: geo_trade

I will estimate the causal effect by two-stage least squares (2SLS), using assignment to the 1980 regional customs pilot (customs_draw) as an instrument for a country's trade share (exports+imports as % GDP), because the pilot randomly halved border fees and the memo states it "changed nothing else." In the first stage I will regress trade share on customs_draw plus covariates (log population, log land_area, landlocked dummy, region fixed effects) and in the second stage regress log income per person on the predicted trade share and the same controls. Key variables: treatment = trade share (exports+imports/GDP), outcome = log income per person, instrument = customs_draw; I will cluster SEs at the country level and report weak-instrument–robust inference (Anderson–Rubin/Critical–Value–robust CIs). Because customs_draw is missing for most countries, I will explicitly estimate the 2SLS on the subsample with instrument data and compare OLS on full sample to assess external validity. The main threat is a weak instrument and limited sample/external validity (first-stage F≈2); I will therefore report first-stage diagnostics, perform placebo/balance tests on pre-treatment outcomes, and present results robust to weak-IV methods.  
CANDIDATES:
customs_draw | plausible
geo_trade | violated
landlocked | doubtful
land_area | doubtful
population | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: customs_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect with two-stage least squares using the archdiocese tuition_draw random draw (available for the 1978 pilot subsample) as an instrument for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade, controlling for baseline covariates (female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, region) and clustering standard errors by the original school sampling unit; the outcome is an indicator for graduation by 1984. Key variables are: treatment = attended Catholic high school (10th grade), outcome = graduated by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and controls = baseline demographics and test_10 to improve precision and account for remaining imbalance within the pilot. I will check first-stage strength (reporting the F-statistic), test overidentification if additional exogenous variation is available in the pilot, and estimate bounds and weak-instrument–robust inference (e.g., Anderson-Rubin) to address weak relevance. I will restrict the main IV estimates to the pilot subsample for identification and report reduced-form and intent-to-treat effects for transparency. The main threat is a weak instrument and very limited external validity because tuition_draw is missing for most students and increases Catholic enrollment by only about 2 percentage points (first-stage F≈2), which can produce imprecise or misleading IV estimates even if exclusion holds. I will also assess heterogeneous effects and conduct sensitivity analyses (placebo outcomes, covariate balance, and bounding) before drawing causal conclusions.

CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated
urban | doubtful
region | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: tuition_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect by two-stage least squares using the 1978 archdiocese pilot random draw for a Catholic high‑school tuition voucher (tuition_draw) as an instrument for attending a Catholic high school, restricting the sample to the pilot-area cohort so the draw approximates random assignment and clustering SEs at the original school. Key variables will be: treatment = attended a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = graduated by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and baseline covariates for precision (female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, catholic_relig, urban, region); I will report first-stage F, use weak‑IV robust inference (LIML and CLR), and present the IV estimate as a LATE for compliers. The main threat is a weak instrument (first-stage F ≈ 2) and the small, pilot-only sample (plus data-use suppression rules) that limit power and external validity; I will therefore present weak‑instrument‑robust confidence intervals, conduct balance and placebo checks, and report intent‑to‑treat estimates as robustness. CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated
region | doubtful
urban | doubtful

I will estimate a local average treatment effect using the randomized 1978 archdiocese tuition voucher draw (tuition_draw) as an instrument for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade and implement IV (two-stage least squares) restricted to the pilot subsample where tuition_draw is observed. Key variables are: treatment = indicator for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = indicator for graduating from high school by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and baseline covariates (female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, catholic_relig, urban, region) to improve precision and test balance. The voucher draw was randomized and is reported to have changed only Catholic-HS attendance, so exclusion is plausible in the pilot sample and IV estimates the effect for compliers. The main threat is the very weak first stage (first-stage F ≈ 2), which yields imprecise and potentially biased IV estimates and limits power and credibility. I will therefore report first-stage diagnostics, use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin and LIML), show OLS with rich controls as a benchmark, and assess heterogeneity (e.g., by catholic_relig and test_10) and external-validity limits.

CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated
region | doubtful
urban | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: tuition_draw

I will estimate the local average treatment effect of attending a Catholic high school using the 1978 archdiocese tuition-voucher random draw (tuition_draw) as an instrument for actual attendance and implement two-stage least squares with weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin/CLR) and school-clustered standard errors, restricting the main analysis to the pilot cities/cohort where tuition_draw is defined. Key variables are instrument = tuition_draw, treatment = attended a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = graduated from high school by 1984, with baseline covariates (female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, region) and missingness flags included to improve precision and test balance. I will report first-stage statistics (F-stat), present weak-instrument-robust confidence sets, and run sensitivity checks including OLS, IV with/without covariates, balance tests by draw, and bounding for selection/attrition. I will cluster inference at the school level, test for differential attrition or other changes in pilot areas (the program memo claims the voucher changed nothing else), and interpret estimates as a LATE for compliers in the pilot sample. The main threat is the very weak first stage (F ≈ 2) which makes standard IV inference unreliable and leaves estimates imprecise, plus possible violations of exclusion if the draw affected follow-up or other unobserved channels despite the memo. CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated
region | doubtful
urban | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: tuition_draw

I will estimate a local average treatment effect with two-stage least squares (2SLS), using the archdiocese random draw (tuition_draw) as an encouragement instrument for attending a Catholic high school and clustering SEs at the school level. Key variables are: treatment = indicator for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = graduated by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and precision covariates = female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, region, and catholic_relig. I will restrict the analysis to the subsample where tuition_draw is observed (the 8th-grade pilot cities), report the first-stage coefficient and F-statistic, and use weak-IV-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin or LIML) while also presenting the intent-to-treat (reduced-form) estimates. The principal identifying assumption is that the random draw affects graduation only through increased probability of attending a Catholic high school (the agency notes the voucher "changed nothing else"), and I will test balance of baseline covariates by draw to support exclusion. The main threat is the very weak first stage (draw raises Catholic attendance by only ~2 percentage points, F≈2), producing imprecise and potentially biased IV estimates and limiting external validity to the drawn subsample. I will therefore supplement IV with reduced-form, bounding, and sensitivity analyses and transparently report subgroup sample sizes and the weak-IV diagnostics.
CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated
urban | doubtful
region | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: tuition_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (IV), exploiting the random 1978 archdiocese tuition voucher draw (tuition_draw) as an instrument for attending a Catholic high school and restricting the sample to students in the pilot cities while including baseline covariates and school fixed effects. Key variables are treatment = attended a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = graduated by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and controls = female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, and region. I will cluster standard errors at the school (or randomization) level, report first-stage diagnostics, and use weak-instrument-robust inference (e.g., Anderson–Rubin) and present the LATE estimate for compliers. The main threat is a weak instrument (first-stage F ≈ 2) that yields imprecise or biased IV estimates and limits power and external validity to the pilot compliers. The agency note that the voucher "changed nothing else" supports the exclusion restriction, but I will run balance tests and placebo outcome checks and report sensitivity/bounds.  
CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (IV) exploiting the archdiocese pilot random draw (tuition_draw) as an instrument for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade, and report both the reduced-form (ITT) and the LATE. Key variables: instrument = tuition_draw; treatment = attended a Catholic high school in 10th grade; outcome = graduated from high school by 1984; baseline controls = female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, region, and school/sampling-unit fixed effects; cluster standard errors at the school level. Because the draw applies only to 8th-graders in 12 pilot cities I will restrict the main IV sample to those pilot-area observations (and show full-sample robustness), and I will verify balance of baseline covariates by draw. Given the reported weak first-stage (F≈2) I will report the first-stage, use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin and LIML), and present ITT estimates and conservative bounds to reflect imprecision. The main threat is a weak instrument and resulting imprecise, local estimate (and limited external validity), although program documentation that the voucher "changed nothing else" supports the exclusion restriction and I will test for any residual imbalance.  
CANDIDATES:
tuition_draw | plausible
catholic_relig | violated

I will estimate a local average treatment effect using two-stage least squares (IV) with the random 1978 archdiocese tuition_draw as the instrument for attending a Catholic high school, restricting the sample to the 12-city pilot where tuition_draw is observed. Key variables are treatment = indicator for attending a Catholic high school in 10th grade, outcome = graduated by 1984, instrument = tuition_draw, and baseline controls (female, parent_ed, fam_income, test_10, urban, region, catholic_relig) with SEs clustered at the school level to account for the sampling design. Because the reported first-stage is weak (F≈2) I will report first-stage statistics, use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin / LIML), and present OLS and IV bounds. I will check randomization balance on pre-treatment covariates, examine attrition and measurement error in graduation, and limit inference to compliers in the pilot cities to be transparent about external validity. The main threat is the weak instrument and consequent imprecision or bias if the exclusion restriction is imperfect or if draw affects graduation through channels other than Catholic attendance; sensitivity checks and alternative inference methods will address this. If the instrument proves unusably weak I will report credible bounds and descriptive heterogeneity instead of a point IV estimate.

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (2SLS) with state and year fixed effects, instrumenting the annual increase in rural bank branches per 100,000 people with the 1981 central-bank random draw (fee_draw) that waived licensing fees for drawn states during 1982–1990. The outcome is the state-year share of the rural population below the poverty line and the endogenous treatment is rural branches opened per 100,000 people; I will include time-varying controls (state_income, literacy, land_ineq) and state-specific linear trends. I will cluster standard errors at the state level and report first-stage F-statistics, weak-instrument-robust CIs (e.g., Anderson-Rubin), and placebo pre-trend tests. As a robustness check I will report estimates using post77_x_fin61 as an alternative instrument and in reduced samples (1982–1990) to assess consistency. The main threat is weak instrument bias and limited external validity because fee_draw affects only 1982–1990 and the first-stage is weak (reported F≈2), and a secondary threat is that the post-1977 instrument may violate exclusion due to contemporaneous redistribution of anti-poverty spending to states with low 1961 branch density.

CANDIDATES:
fee_draw | plausible
post77_x_fin61 | violated
INSTRUMENT: fee_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using an IV/2SLS design that exploits the central bank's 1981 random draw (fee_draw) which waived branch licensing fees in drawn states for 1982–1990 as an instrument for the state-year rural branches opened per 100,000 people; the second stage will regress the rural poverty share on the predicted branch openings with state and year fixed effects and clustered SEs. Key variables are the endogenous regressor (rural branches opened per 100k), the outcome (share of rural population below the poverty line), controls (state_income, literacy, land_ineq, rural_pop) and the instrument fee_draw; I will report first-stage F-statistics and use weak-instrument-robust CIs as needed. As a robustness check I will also instrument with post77_x_fin61 (the interaction of 1961 branch density and years since 1977) in the 1977–1989 window and run event-study/pre-trend tests to compare dynamics. I will test balance on pre-trends and on observable covariates and run placebo outcomes and time-by-state falsification checks. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction via contemporaneous state-level policies targeted to states with low 1961 branch density (which compromises post77_x_fin61) and low power from a weak first stage for fee_draw.

CANDIDATES:
post77_x_fin61 | doubtful
fee_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: fee_draw

I will estimate the causal effect with an IV difference-in-differences: instrument state-year rural branches per 100,000 (treatment) with post77_x_fin61 (1961 branches per person × years since 1977) exploiting the 1977 licensing rule, while including state and year fixed effects and state-specific linear trends. Key variables are the outcome (share of rural population below the poverty line), the treatment (rural bank branches per 100,000, lagged one period), and the instrument (post77_x_fin61); I will control for state_income, literacy, land_ineq, rural_pop and cluster standard errors by state. Estimation is two-stage least squares with first-stage F-statistics reported and robustness checks that use the 1981 fee-waiver random draw (fee_draw) as an alternative instrument, run reduced-form checks, and weight observations by rural population where appropriate. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because lagging states (low 1961 branches per person) were targeted for higher antipoverty spending in 1978–80 and may have had other concurrent policies or shocks affecting poverty. I will address this by controlling for available state fiscal transfers, conducting pre-trend and placebo outcome tests before 1977, and showing robustness to excluding lagging states and adding time-varying covariates. If these diagnostics leave the exclusion restriction doubtful I will report reduced-form effects and IV bounds instead of a single causal point estimate.

CANDIDATES:
post77_x_fin61 | plausible
fee_draw | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: post77_x_fin61

I will estimate a causal effect using an instrumental-variables (2SLS) design that exploits the central bank's 1981 random draw waiver of branch licensing fees (fee_draw) to instrument for exogenous increases in rural bank branches per 100,000 people and regress the rural poverty share on the instrumented branch density with state and year fixed effects. Key variables are the outcome (share of rural population below the poverty line), the endogenous treatment (rural bank branches per 100,000), the instrument (fee_draw), and controls for state_income, literacy, land_ineq, rural_pop and baseline trends to improve precision. I will restrict the main IV sample to the 1982–1990 window when the waiver applied, report first-stage strength and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin/LIML), and run reduced-form and placebo checks; as a robustness check I will also estimate an alternative IV using post77_x_fin61 and compare estimates. The main threat is a weak first stage and the short time window for fee_draw (F≈2), plus potential heterogeneous spillovers or concurrent targeted anti-poverty programs that could confound alternative instruments, so I will present weak-IV-robust confidence intervals and sensitivity analyses.

The treatment variable is rural bank branches per 100,000 and the outcome is the share of the rural population below the poverty line; I will include controls (rural_pop, state_income, literacy, land_ineq) and cluster standard errors at the state level. The primary threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if 1961 branch density is correlated with unobserved, time-varying determinants of poverty (persistent development differences) that affect poverty independent of branch expansion; I will mitigate this with pre-treatment balance checks, controls for pre-1977 levels, and sensitivity analyses.

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares with state and year fixed effects: first stage instruments rural branches opened in unbanked rural locations (per 100,000) with the central bank's 1981 random draw that waived licensing fees (fee_draw) for 1982–1990, and the second stage estimates the effect of predicted branch expansion on the rural poverty share. Key variables are the outcome (share of rural population below the poverty line), the treatment (rural branches opened per 100,000 people), the instrument (fee_draw), and controls including rural_pop, state_income, literacy, land_ineq and state-specific linear trends; I will report OLS, IV (2SLS), and weak‑instrument robust inference (e.g., LIML, Anderson-Rubin). As robustness checks I will (a) restrict to 1982–1990 for the randomized instrument, (b) use the post77_x_fin61 interaction (pre-1977 branch density × post-1977 period) as an alternative instrument in the full 1961–2000 sample and a difference-in-differences design exploiting the 1977 licensing rule, and (c) test for pre-trend balance and include controls for targeted anti-poverty spending where available. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction because planning commission records show anti-poverty programs (1978–1980) directed more resources to the lagging states identified by 1961 branch density, and the randomized fee_draw instrument is weak (first-stage F≈2), so results may be biased or imprecise. To mitigate I will test balance, control for pre-existing trends and targeted transfers, report weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals, and present bounds and sensitivity analyses.

fee_draw | plausible
